title: The Lunar Disc: Features, Rotation and Libration
description: Naming lunar features, the synchronous orbit and how libration lets us see slightly more than half the Moon's surface.
content_html:
Our Nearest Neighbour

The Moon is Earth’s only natural satellite and the most studied body in the night sky. Its mean diameter is approximately 3 500 km — roughly a quarter of Earth’s mean diameter. Even with the naked eye you can see broad bright and dark patches across its face; through binoculars or a small telescope a stunning world of craters, mountains and ancient lava plains comes into view.

Types of Lunar Feature

The lunar surface is divided into two broad terrain types. The bright, rugged highland regions are called terrae (singular: terra). These ancient rocks record billions of years of meteorite bombardment. The darker, lower-lying regions are the maria (singular: mare). Despite their watery name, the maria are vast plains of solidified basaltic lava that flooded low-lying impact basins between roughly 3 and 4 billion years ago. They appear darker because basalt reflects less sunlight than highland rock.

Three named maria you are expected to know are the Sea of Tranquility (Mare Tranquillitatis — landing site of Apollo 11 in 1969), the Ocean of Storms (Oceanus Procellarum — the largest dark region, visible to the naked eye) and the Sea of Crises (Mare Crisium — a nearly circular mare in the north-east quadrant of the near side).

The lunar surface also bears mountains and valleys. The most prominent range is the Apennine mountain range, which arcs around the south-eastern rim of Mare Imbrium and contains peaks exceeding 5 km in height — comparable to the European Alps.

Named Craters

Craters cover most of the lunar surface. Three prominent craters form a useful observational triangle near the southern highlands:

  • Tycho — a young, bright crater in the southern highlands, famous for its spectacular ray system that stretches thousands of kilometres across the surface. The rays are ejected material blasted out at impact and are most visible at full moon.
  • Copernicus — a large, well-preserved impact crater with a terraced inner wall and central peaks, located in the Oceanus Procellarum region. Roughly 93 km in diameter.
  • Kepler — a smaller but well-defined crater west of Copernicus, also showing a bright ray system.
Key Fact

Key named features: Maria (Sea of Tranquility, Ocean of Storms, Sea of Crises); Craters (Tycho — youngest rays; Copernicus — terraced walls; Kepler — bright rays); Mountains (Apennine range, peaks to 5 km).

Synchronous Rotation and Tidal Locking

If you observe the Moon over many nights, you will notice that it always shows the same face. This is not a coincidence — it is the result of tidal locking (also called synchronous rotation). The Moon’s rotation period (the time it takes to spin once on its axis) is 27.3 days, which is exactly equal to its revolution period (the time it takes to complete one orbit of Earth). Billions of years of tidal friction — gravitational tugging between Earth and the Moon’s slightly non-uniform mass — gradually slowed the Moon’s spin until the two periods matched and stabilised.

The result is that the near side of the Moon always faces Earth, while the far side — sometimes called the ‘dark side’ (a misleading label, since it receives just as much sunlight as the near side) — was never seen by humans until the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft photographed it in 1959.

The far side receives sunlight for approximately half its month, just as the near side does. The term ‘dark side’ is sometimes used loosely to mean ‘the side we cannot see from Earth’. In exam answers, call it the far side to avoid confusion — examiners expect precise terminology. The far side is actually more heavily cratered than the near side because a thicker crust prevented the volcanic flooding that created the near side’s maria.

Libration: Peeking Around the Edge

Although we always see the same face of the Moon on average, we can actually observe slightly more than 50% of its total surface over time. This effect is called libration. There are three main causes:

  • Libration in longitude: The Moon travels in an elliptical orbit so its speed varies — faster at perigee (closest point) and slower at apogee (furthest point). Its spin rate, however, is constant. This mismatch means the Moon appears to rock from side to side slightly, letting us peek around its eastern and western limbs alternately.
  • Libration in latitude: The Moon’s equator is tilted slightly with respect to its orbital plane, so it nods gently north and south during each orbit, exposing a little of each polar region in turn.
  • Diurnal libration: Because Earth rotates, an observer shifts position between moonrise and moonset, viewing the Moon from slightly different angles and seeing marginally around one limb or the other.

Combined, librations allow us to observe approximately 59% of the lunar surface over time, rather than exactly 50%.

Key Fact

Libration allows about 59% of the Moon’s surface to be seen from Earth over time. There are three types: libration in longitude (elliptical orbit speed variation), libration in latitude (axial tilt of the Moon) and diurnal libration (observer’s shift as Earth rotates).

The best time to observe craters is not at full moon, despite the Moon being brightest then. At full moon, sunlight falls almost straight down onto the surface, leaving craters without shadows and making them hard to distinguish. The best views come in the days around first quarter (waxing crescent / quarter phase) when the terminator — the line between lit and unlit hemispheres — crosses the surface. Here, low-angle sunlight casts long, dramatic shadows across crater rims and mountain peaks. The exception is ray craters like Tycho and Copernicus, which are actually most prominent at full moon because their bright ejecta rays reflect a great deal of sunlight.
exam_tip_html: Exam questions on the Moon frequently ask you to name specific features — learn all three named maria, all three named craters and the Apennine range. For questions on tidal locking, be precise: the rotation period equals the orbital period (both 27.3 days). Do not say the Moon ‘doesn’t rotate’ — it does rotate once per orbit. For libration questions, state the type and its specific cause. If asked why we can observe 59% rather than 50%, name all three libration types for full marks. Never call the far side the ‘dark side’ in an exam answer — use the correct term.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Moon (mean diameter ~3 500 km) has two main terrain types: bright terrae (highlands) and dark maria (ancient lava plains). Named features include the Sea of Tranquility, Ocean of Storms, Sea of Crises, Tycho, Copernicus, Kepler and the Apennine mountains.
  • Tidal locking means the Moon’s rotation period equals its orbital period (27.3 days), so the same face always points toward Earth. The far side (not ‘dark side’) was first photographed in 1959.
  • Libration — in longitude, in latitude and diurnal — allows approximately 59% of the total lunar surface to be observed from Earth over time.

practice_questions.text:
What is the approximate mean diameter of the Moon?
A) 1 200 km
B) 3 500 km
C) 6 400 km
D) 12 700 km
Name the type of lunar terrain formed by ancient lava flows.
State what is meant by tidal locking (synchronous rotation) and give the value of the Moon's orbital period.
practice_questions.marks: Tidal locking means the Moon's rotation period equals its orbital period [1]; the orbital (and rotation) period is 27.3 days [1].

practice_questions.text: The Holt Astronomy Group, observing from Norfolk, notices that the Moon appears to rock slightly from side to side over several weeks, exposing regions near its eastern and western edges that are not normally visible. Explain the cause of this phenomenon.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names the phenomenon as libration in longitude [1]; explains that the Moon's orbital speed varies because its orbit is elliptical — faster at perigee, slower at apogee [1]; states that because the spin rate is constant but the orbital speed is not, the Moon appears to rock east-west, exposing limb regions [1].
Secure: Identifies libration and one correct cause.
Developing: Mentions libration without explaining the elliptical orbit mechanism.
Emerging: No credit-worthy content.

practice_questions.text: Compare the terrae and maria of the Moon, referring to their appearance, composition and origin.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Terrae are bright, rugged, ancient highlands made of lighter highland rock [1], heavily cratered from meteorite bombardment over billions of years [1]; WHEREAS maria are darker, flatter plains of solidified basaltic lava [1] that flooded low-lying impact basins approximately 3-4 billion years ago [1].
Secure: Three of four marking points.
Developing: Describes one terrain type only.
Emerging: Vague or one brief correct statement.

practice_questions.text:
Marina Vassilakis, an astronomy enthusiast in Glasgow, wants to observe and sketch the crater Tycho and the Apennine mountain range in a single observing session. Design an observation plan for her, including the optimal phase of the Moon to choose and the reasons for your choices. In your answer, discuss equipment, observing conditions and what she should expect to record.

Your answer should include a discussion of at least three distinct points.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): States that the terminator region at first quarter or a few days after provides the best shadowing for crater and mountain detail [1]; explains that low-angle sunlight at the terminator casts long shadows revealing relief [1]; notes that full moon is not ideal for craters (flat lighting, no shadows) but that Tycho's rays are brightest at full moon — candidate may address this subtlety [1]; recommends binoculars (7x50 or similar) or a small telescope [1]; mentions recording conditions (seeing quality, transparency, light pollution), sketching or timing, and noting the date and time to identify the Moon's phase precisely [1]; discusses potential challenges for Glasgow: cloud cover, city light pollution, Moon altitude at time of observation [1].
Secure (3-4): Correct phase recommendation with at least two well-explained factors.
Developing (1-2): Mentions equipment or phase without clear justification.
Emerging (0): No credit-worthy content.

knowledge_checks.q: What are the dark, flat lowland plains of the Moon called?
Which crater is known for its spectacular bright ray system stretching thousands of kilometres?
The Moon's rotation period is ___ days, which is equal to its orbital period.
Libration means that we can observe approximately ___% of the Moon's total surface over time.
Match each lunar feature to its description:
right: Mountain range with peaks exceeding 5 km

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate mean diameter of the Moon?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 3 500 km — about a quarter of Earth's diameter.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the terrae on the Moon?
flashcard_questions.a: Bright, heavily cratered highland regions formed of ancient rock.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the maria on the Moon?
flashcard_questions.a: Dark, flat plains of solidified basaltic lava that flooded ancient impact basins.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three named maria you must know.
flashcard_questions.a: Sea of Tranquility, Ocean of Storms, Sea of Crises.

flashcard_questions.q: Which named crater has the most prominent ray system at full moon?
flashcard_questions.a: Tycho — young crater in the southern highlands with rays extending thousands of km.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Apennine mountain range, and where is it?
flashcard_questions.a: A lunar mountain range bordering Mare Imbrium, with peaks over 5 km.
When the Moon's rotation period equals its orbital period (27.3 days), keeping one face toward Earth.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should the far side of the Moon not be called the 'dark side'?
flashcard_questions.a: The far side receives as much sunlight as the near side — it is simply not visible from Earth.
An apparent rocking of the Moon that allows about 59% of its surface to be seen from Earth over time.
The Moon's orbital speed varies (elliptical orbit) but its spin rate is constant, causing apparent east-west rocking.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the best lunar phase to observe crater detail and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Near first quarter — the terminator casts long shadows revealing crater walls and mountain peaks.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Soviet spacecraft first photographed the far side of the Moon?

glossary_terms.definition: The bright, heavily cratered highland regions of the Moon's surface; the Latin word for 'lands'.
The dark, relatively flat lowland plains of the Moon formed by ancient volcanic flooding; the Latin word for 'seas'.
A roughly circular depression on the Moon's surface formed by the impact of a meteorite or asteroid.
A mountain range on the Moon bordering the eastern edge of Mare Imbrium, containing peaks over 5 km high.
When a satellite's rotation period equals its orbital period, so it always keeps the same hemisphere facing its parent body.
A slight apparent rocking or wobbling of the Moon as seen from Earth, allowing observers to see a little beyond each limb at different times.
The line on the Moon separating the sunlit hemisphere from the shadowed hemisphere, where crater shadows are longest and most dramatic.
